design_rationale: Participants were explicitly allocated to experimental and control groups by drawing lots, which is a random allocation mechanism.

domain_judgments.rationale: Allocation by drawing lots was random, but concealment procedures were not reported and caregivers had a statistically significant baseline imbalance in biological relationship.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: After their written consent was obtained, the participants were randomly assigned to experimental and control groups by drawing lots.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants necessarily knew whether they attended psychoeducation, and the stated post-randomization exclusion of participants attending less than 70% could produce a per-protocol effect estimate rather than an intention-to-treat estimate, although no participants were ultimately reported as lost.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Those with less than a 70% attendance rate for any reason were excluded from the study.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome data were reported as complete for all randomized client-caregiver pairs through 12 months, with no attrition or dropouts.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: There was no attrition in this study.

domain_judgments.rationale: Validated measures were administered consistently by a nurse independent of intervention delivery, but assessor blinding to assignment was not stated and several outcomes were subjective self-reports susceptible to participants' awareness of intervention status.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: All the pre- and post-tests were conducted by an assigned mental health nurse who was not involved in the intervention to avoid bias.

domain_judgments.rationale: No preregistration or prespecified analysis plan was reported, while numerous outcomes, time points, and both repeated-measures and time-specific tests created scope for selective reporting.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A multivariate repeated measured ANOVA was performed to examine the differences between the two groups over time with the adjustment of age and sex. The differences between the individual outcome variables at each time point were assessed by the Mann– Whitney U-test.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by the protocol allowing post-randomization exclusion for inadequate attendance and the absence of a clearly reported intention-to-treat analysis. Additional concerns arise from unreported allocation concealment, lack of stated assessor blinding for subjective outcomes, and no preregistered analysis plan.

design_rationale: The study explicitly states that 70 caregiver–patient dyads were randomly allocated to experimental and control groups, although the sequence-generation and concealment methods are not described.

domain_judgments.rationale: Random allocation and blinded assignment are asserted, and measured baseline characteristics were similar, but neither sequence generation nor allocation concealment is adequately described.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Seventy caregivers patients with schizophrenia whose records were available at three psychiatric centers in Shiraz were randomized blindly to two groups

domain_judgments.rationale: Caregivers necessarily knew whether they attended psychoeducation, adherence appears complete among analyzed intervention participants, but the analysis excluded five randomized dropouts rather than clearly using intention-to-treat and provides limited information on other deviations.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A total of 65 families completed the study. Five participants (two from the experimental group and three from the control group) dropped out before completion of the study

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome data were available for 65 of 70 randomized families (92.9%), attrition was small and balanced between groups, and the stated reasons were unrelated to the study.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Five participants (two from the experimental group and three from the control group) dropped out before completion of the study for different reasons unrelated to the study.

domain_judgments.rationale: Although validated scales were applied at the same times and a co-researcher was described as blinded, both psychiatric symptoms and caregiver burden were completed by caregivers who necessarily knew their assignment, making the subjective outcomes vulnerable to differential reporting, especially because caregiver burden directly concerns their own experience.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Data were collected with a personal information sheet, the Iranian version of the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) [29] which was completed for every patient by caregiver, and the Family Burden questionnaire [25].

domain_judgments.rationale: A trial registration number is reported, but no prospective protocol or prespecified analysis plan is presented, and several BPRS subscales, time points, and statistical effects offered multiple eligible results for selection.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Trial registration: IRCT Number:138809122812 N1

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high because subjective psychiatric-symptom and caregiver-burden outcomes were reported by unblinded caregivers, creating substantial potential for differential outcome measurement. Additional concerns arise from insufficiently described randomization/concealment, complete-case rather than clearly intention-to-treat analysis, and limited evidence of prespecified outcome analysis.

design_rationale: Participants were explicitly allocated to the BPI and nonspecific control groups using random allocation tables.

domain_judgments.rationale: A random allocation table was used, but allocation concealment was not described, serial enrollment could permit foreknowledge, and some sizable baseline QOL differences raise concern despite the authors' statement that groups were comparable.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: These participants were assigned serial numbers in order of their inclusion in the study. They were then randomly allocated to the BPI group and nonspecific control intervention group (NCI group), using random allocation tables.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and intervention providers were necessarily aware of assignment, intervention adherence was poor, and the analysis excluded nonadherent participants rather than following intention-to-treat, which could bias effects.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Out of the 33 included in the BPI group, 24 were eligible for the final assessment having attended two psycho‑education sessions and at least two group therapy sessions. Out of the 33 patients and family members included in the NCI group, 23 were eligible for the final assessment.

domain_judgments.rationale: Primary caregiver outcomes were available for only 24/33 intervention and 23/33 control dyads, with additional missing patient outcomes, and there was no convincing analysis showing that missingness could not bias results.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The other major setback in the present study was the poor attendance which is evidenced by the high number of dropouts in both groups, despite the investigator’s repeated attempts to persuade key relatives to attend the sessions.

domain_judgments.rationale: The main caregiver outcomes were subjective self-reports in an unblinded behavioral trial, so respondents' knowledge of receiving the active intervention could plausibly influence reported burden and quality of life; assessor blinding was also not adequately described.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Evaluation of patients on the PANSS and WHO‑QOL‑BREF and of their key relatives on BAS and WHO‑QOL‑100 was conducted in both the groups before the start of intervention.

domain_judgments.rationale: No protocol, trial registration, or prespecified analysis plan is reported, while several instruments, domains, and within- and between-group analyses created opportunities for selective reporting, although the main outcome tables are fairly comprehensive.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Analysis of changes in the PANSS, WHO‑QOL‑BREF, BAS, and WHOQOL‑100 scores, before and after BPI/NCI sessions, was done by using paired “t‑” test.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by exclusion of many randomized participants/non-intention-to-treat analysis, substantial missing outcome data, and subjective outcomes reported by unblinded participants. Allocation concealment and prespecification of analyses were also insufficiently documented.

design_rationale: The study explicitly reports random assignment of 48 consenting caregivers to intervention or control by drawing a number from a sealed opaque envelope.

domain_judgments.rationale: Allocation was explicitly random and concealed using sealed opaque envelopes after baseline assessment, and the reported baseline characteristics and outcome measures showed no important evidence of imbalance beyond chance.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Subjects were then randomized to experimental or control group by drawing a number from a sealed opaque envelope.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and the facilitator knew allocation, three intervention participants attended fewer than seven sessions, and the intervention group was instructed to avoid other family therapy; although fidelity was monitored and all randomized participants were analyzed, the unblinded context could have produced intervention-related deviations.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Only the principal researcher (who was also the group facilitator) and the subjects themselves were aware of the group to which they had been allocated.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome data were available for all 48 randomized participants at follow-up, including the three intervention participants who did not meet the attendance threshold, and all were included in the analysis.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: No subject was lost to follow-up and thus all 48 subjects were included in the final data analysis.

domain_judgments.rationale: Validated measures were administered consistently by a research assistant who appears blinded to allocation, and rehospitalization came from clinic records; however, key caregiver-reported outcomes were subjective and participants knew their intervention status, allowing expectancy and socially desirable responding to influence measurements.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Finally, by virtue of group membership, those in the experimental group may have perceived themselves as having received more care and attention than their control counterparts. This may, in turn, have influenced their responses to the intervention and their scores on the outcome measures.

domain_judgments.rationale: No preregistration or prespecified statistical analysis plan is reported, while several outcomes, subscales, time points, and possible analyses were available, creating scope for selective reporting despite presentation of all four principal outcomes.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Three outcome measures were included within the questionnaires administered by the independent research assistant to the subjects in the intervention and control group both pre- and post-intervention.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is judged as some concerns. Randomization, allocation concealment, complete follow-up, and intention-to-treat analysis were strengths, but participant awareness and subjective self-reported outcomes, possible intervention-related deviations, and the absence of preregistration or a prespecified analysis plan leave concerns.

design_rationale: The study explicitly reports random allocation of 96 families to three conditions using sealed opaque envelopes containing numbered group assignments.

domain_judgments.rationale: Allocation concealment was plausibly maintained with sealed opaque envelopes and baseline characteristics were balanced, but the method used to generate the intervention-allocation sequence and safeguards such as envelope numbering were not reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Participants were then asked to draw a sealed opaque envelope in which a number card indicated to which group they had been allocated (1 = mutual support, 2 = psycho-education, 3 = standard care).

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and intervention providers necessarily knew the behavioral treatment received, and the principal researcher delivered or assisted both active interventions with acknowledged differential enthusiasm risk, although intervention fidelity was monitored and intention-to-treat analysis was reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The principal researcher involved in leading the two intervention groups might have been biased in favour of the mutual support group intervention.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome assessments were reported for all randomized participants at all three time points, including intervention dropouts and nonattenders.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: These people, together with those who dropped out or were absent for more than four sessions [mutual support group (n = 5), psycho-education group (n = 2) and standard care group (n = 1)], were also evaluated at three times.

domain_judgments.rationale: Although validated measures and an independent assessor were used consistently, the key family and patient functioning outcomes were caregiver-reported, caregivers could not be blinded, and the authors explicitly recognized possible socially desirable responses favoring the researcher, making differential measurement bias likely for subjective outcomes.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: This is also important to reduce socially desirable responses by participants in favour of the researchers and may increase the reliability of their responses.

domain_judgments.rationale: No preregistration or prespecified statistical analysis plan is reported, while numerous scales, subscales, time points, and post-hoc comparisons created scope for selective choice among eligible results despite reporting both significant and nonsignificant outcomes.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Post-hoc analysis using Tukey’s Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) test for multiple comparisons was performed for those measures that indicated a statistically significant interaction effect for time-by-programme in the MANOVAs.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by likely differential measurement bias in subjective caregiver-reported outcomes when participants knew their assignment and may have responded favorably to the researcher who delivered the interventions. Additional concerns arise from incompletely described sequence generation, possible intervention-delivery bias, and lack of a prespecified analysis plan.

design_rationale: This was an explicitly randomized controlled trial in which consenting caregiver–patient pairs were allocated by drawing a number from a sealed opaque envelope.

domain_judgments.rationale: Allocation by drawing labeled cards from an opaque envelope was intended to be random and baseline characteristics were similar, but the sequence-generating composition and handling of the envelope were insufficiently described to establish robust sequence generation and concealment.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: After consent to participate was obtained, they were assigned randomly to one of the study groups by drawing a number from a sealed opaque envelope.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants knew their assignment and three intervention participants attended fewer than half of the sessions, although fidelity was monitored, controls received usual care, and an intention-to-treat analysis retained all randomized participants.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Three caregivers in the mutual support group were terminated because they failed to attend a minimum of seven group sessions (i.e., less than 50% group attendance).

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome data were available for all 76 randomized participants at follow-up, including the three intervention participants with poor attendance.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: No subject was lost at follow-up and thus all 76 subjects were included in the final data analysis.

domain_judgments.rationale: Most key family outcomes were self-reported by unblinded caregivers, and the first author/research team—aware of assignment and involved in intervention delivery—administered outcome measures, making differential measurement plausible; record-based rehospitalization was more objective but does not remove this concern for the principal psychosocial outcomes.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Only the researcher and the participants were aware of the group to which they had been assigned.

domain_judgments.rationale: No prespecified protocol or statistical analysis plan is reported, while six outcomes, subscales, repeated time points, and several multivariate, univariate, and contrast analyses created scope for selective reporting, despite the paper reporting both significant and nonsignificant outcomes.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: For the four variables (FBIS, FAD, SSQ6, and duration of patients’ re-hospitalization) that showed significant difference between groups, Helmert contrasts test (univariate) was conducted to test any significant differences in mean scores of each variable within group as well as between groups at the 12-month follow-up.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high because the principal psychosocial outcomes were self-reported and administered without assessor or participant blinding, creating substantial potential for intervention-aware measurement bias. Additional concerns arise from incompletely described allocation procedures, intervention nonadherence, and absence of a prespecified analysis plan, although follow-up was complete.

design_rationale: The study explicitly reports random assignment of consenting families to psychoeducation/support or routine care, implemented by drawing sealed opaque envelopes indicating group allocation.

domain_judgments.rationale: Allocation used sealed opaque envelopes, but the method used to generate the intervention-allocation sequence and safeguards such as sequential numbering were not reported, and the principal researcher administered allocation; moreover, the reported patient mean ages differed substantially between groups despite claims of baseline comparability.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: the participants were then asked by the principal researcher to draw a sealed opaque envelope, in which a number card indicated to which group they had been allocated (1 = psycho-education group and 2 = routine care group).

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants necessarily knew whether they attended the intensive behavioral group, but intervention delivery was standardized and monitored, co-interventions were similar between groups, and an intention-to-treat analysis retained participants regardless of completion.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Analysis of data was on an intention-to-treat basis [35]. All subjects, who completed the intervention or not, were followed up over a 12-month post-intervention period.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome measurements reportedly included participants who discontinued or had substantial absence, indicating essentially complete follow-up of randomized participants despite a few intervention discontinuations.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: These subjects, together with those who dropped out or absented in more than four group sessions - psycho-education group (n = 3) and routine care group (n = 2), were evaluated at three times of outcome measurements.

domain_judgments.rationale: The instruments were generally validated and an independent assessor was used, but blinding of that assessor is stated only later and most outcomes were participant-reported, so intervention participants aware of assignment could give socially desirable responses, a limitation acknowledged by the authors.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: the family caregivers in the psychoeducation group program might provide socially desirable responses on the outcome measures over the follow-up period because they may well be eager to show appreciation and positive feedback to the health professionals and the research team who have offered additional family support.

domain_judgments.rationale: No preregistration or prespecified analysis plan is reported despite multiple outcomes, subscales, time points, and post-hoc tests, and there are major internal inconsistencies in outcome direction and reporting—for example, higher FAD scores are defined as poorer functioning and increased markedly, yet are interpreted as improvement—creating strong concern that favorable results were selectively interpreted or reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The possible total scores range from 4 to 28, a higher score reflecting poorer functioning of the family.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by high risk in selection of the reported result due to absent prospective specification, extensive multiplicity, and serious inconsistencies between scale direction, tabulated data, and favorable interpretation. Additional concerns arise from incompletely described sequence generation/concealment and potentially socially desirable self-reported outcomes in unblinded participants.
